promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the core of Hume's argument against believing in miracles based on testimony?
options: The wise proportion belief to evidence, and the uniform experience supporting natural laws always outweighs the testimony for a miracle
Religious language is meaningless
God does not exist
Miracles are logically impossible
questions.explain: Hume argues it is always more probable that the testimony is mistaken or false than that a law of nature has genuinely been violated.

questions.q: On Wittgenstein's 'language games' approach, religious language is meaningful because:
options: It is purely negative
It can be empirically verified
It is falsifiable
It functions within its own form of life with rules and purposes, not judged by the criteria of science
questions.explain: Wittgenstein holds that meaning is use; religious language is a distinct language game whose meaning lies within the practice of the believing community.

questions.q: What is distinctive about the Kalam cosmological argument compared with Aquinas's Ways?
options: It argues from design rather than causation
It insists the universe had a beginning in time and so a cause of its beginning
It denies an infinite regress is impossible
It is a priori
questions.explain: The Kalam argument holds that whatever begins to exist has a cause, the universe began to exist, therefore the universe has a cause.

questions.q: The Euthyphro dilemma, often raised against the moral argument, asks:
options: Whether something is good because God commands it, or God commands it because it is good
Whether existence is a predicate
Whether the universe had a beginning
Whether miracles violate natural law
questions.explain: The Euthyphro dilemma challenges divine command theory by asking whether morality is arbitrary (good because commanded) or independent of God.

questions.q: A central claim of Augustine's theodicy is that:
options: God deliberately created evil for soul-making
Evil is a substance created by God
Suffering is an illusion
Evil is a privation (privatio boni), a lack of good, originating in the misuse of free will at the Fall
questions.explain: Augustine holds that evil is not a thing but a privation of good, entering creation through the free fall of angels and humans.

questions.q: In Aquinas's doctrine of analogy, when we say 'God is good', the term 'good' is used:
options: Analogically, neither identical to nor wholly different from its human use
Equivocally, with no shared meaning
Univocally, in exactly the same sense as for humans
As a meaningless symbol
questions.explain: Aquinas argues religious language works by analogy (of attribution and proportion), avoiding both univocal and purely equivocal meaning.

questions.q: What problem famously confronts Descartes' substance dualism, raised by Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia?
options: Whether the Forms are real
Whether animals have souls
Whether God exists
How an immaterial, non-extended mind can causally interact with a material, extended body
questions.explain: The interaction problem questions how a non-physical mind could causally influence a physical body if they are entirely distinct substances.

questions.q: In Plato's Analogy of the Cave, what do the shadows cast on the cave wall represent?
options: The empirical world of appearances perceived by the senses
The Form of the Good
The eternal Forms
The realm of pure intellect
questions.explain: The shadows symbolise the deceptive physical world grasped through the senses, contrasted with the true reality of the Forms.

questions.q: Which of these is one of Hume's criticisms of the design argument?
options: The world is more like a living organism or a vegetable than a designed machine, weakening the analogy
Existence is not a predicate
Moral obligation requires a lawgiver
The universe must have a first cause
questions.explain: Hume challenges the design analogy, suggesting the universe might resemble an organism that grows rather than an artefact that is made.

questions.q: Aquinas's First Way argues from which feature of the world?
options: Degrees of perfection
Motion or change, requiring an unmoved mover
The contingency of beings
The order of nature
questions.explain: The First Way argues from motion/change to an unmoved first mover, since an infinite regress of movers cannot explain motion.

questions.q: What is the central point of Gaunilo's 'perfect island' objection to the ontological argument?
options: That God cannot be defined
That existence cannot be doubted
That the world had a beginning
That the same reasoning would absurdly prove the existence of a perfect island, so the logic must be flawed
questions.explain: Gaunilo parodies Anselm by arguing that if defining the greatest island entailed its existence, we could 'prove' impossible things into being.

questions.q: According to the verification principle of logical positivism, a statement is meaningful only if it is:
options: Emotionally moving
Either analytic (true by definition) or empirically verifiable in principle
Part of a language game
Commanded by God
questions.explain: The verification principle holds that, apart from tautologies, only statements verifiable by sense experience are cognitively meaningful, rendering 'God exists' meaningless to positivists.

questions.q: Aquinas's Third Way (from contingency and necessity) concludes that there must exist:
options: A first temporal moment
A perfectly good being
A necessary being whose existence does not depend on anything else
An intelligent designer
questions.explain: The Third Way argues that contingent beings cannot account for their own existence, so a necessary being must exist to ground them.

questions.q: According to William James in The Varieties of Religious Experience, what are the four marks of mystical experience?
options: Public, repeatable, measurable, verifiable
Ineffable, noetic, transient, passive
Moral, rational, emotional, communal
Numinous, holy, awesome, fearful
questions.explain: James identifies mystical experiences as ineffable, noetic (yielding knowledge), transient, and passive.

questions.q: What is Hume's 'fallacy of composition' objection to the cosmological argument?
options: That the universe is designed
That miracles are improbable
That what is true of the parts (each having a cause) need not be true of the whole universe
That existence is not a predicate
questions.explain: Hume argues it is fallacious to assume the universe as a whole must have a cause simply because each part within it does.

questions.q: Swinburne's principle of credulity states that:
options: All religious experiences are illusory
Only verifiable claims are meaningful
If it seems to a subject that something is present, then probably it is, unless there are special reasons to doubt it
Miracles never occur
questions.explain: The principle of credulity holds that, in the absence of defeaters, we should accept that things are as they appear, including apparent experiences of God.

questions.q: Rudolf Otto's term 'numinous' refers to an experience of:
options: A moral duty
A community ritual
A logical proof of God
A non-rational sense of awe before a 'mysterium tremendum et fascinans', a holy 'wholly other'
questions.explain: The numinous is the felt sense of a holy, awe-inspiring and fascinating divine presence wholly distinct from the self.

questions.q: How does Darwin's theory of natural selection challenge the design argument?
options: By offering a non-purposive, naturalistic explanation for the apparent design and adaptation of organisms
By proving God exists
By showing existence is a perfection
By denying the universe had a beginning
questions.explain: Natural selection explains biological complexity through unguided variation and survival, removing the need to posit a designer.

questions.q: In Descartes' version of the ontological argument, why must existence belong to the concept of a supremely perfect being?
options: Because everyone has an innate idea of causation
Because the world shows evidence of design
Because existence is a perfection, and a supremely perfect being must possess all perfections
Because the universe requires a first cause
questions.explain: Descartes argues that existence is a perfection inseparable from the idea of God, just as having three angles is inseparable from a triangle.

questions.q: Why does Aristotle describe his Prime Mover as a 'final cause' rather than an efficient cause of motion?
options: Because it physically pushes the cosmos into motion
Because it causes motion by being an object of desire, drawing things toward it without itself moving
Because it constantly intervenes in worldly events
Because it created the universe at a point in time
questions.explain: The unmoved Prime Mover causes motion as an object of love and attraction, drawing things toward it while remaining itself unchanged.

questions.q: According to Aristotle, what does the Prime Mover eternally contemplate?
options: The Platonic Forms
The needs of human beings
The created physical world
Itself, since thought thinking itself is the highest activity
questions.explain: Aristotle's Prime Mover engages in 'thought thinking itself' (noesis noeseos), the most perfect activity, and is unaware of the world.

questions.q: What is the role of Plato's Demiurge in the Timaeus?
options: To embody the Form of the Good in human form
To create matter ex nihilo from nothing
To judge souls after death
To fashion the cosmos by imposing order on pre-existing chaotic matter using the Forms as a model
questions.explain: The Demiurge is a craftsman who shapes already-existing matter according to the eternal Forms, rather than creating from nothing.

questions.q: In Kant's moral argument, why must God be postulated?
options: Because of an infinite regress of causes
Because the universe shows design
To guarantee that the summum bonum (union of virtue and happiness) is achievable, which morality requires
Because existence is a perfection
questions.explain: Kant postulates God (and immortality) as necessary conditions for the highest good, in which virtue is ultimately rewarded with happiness.

questions.q: How does Anselm define God in the first form of his ontological argument in the Proslogion?
options: The designer of the natural world
The uncaused cause of the universe
The ground of moral obligation
That than which nothing greater can be conceived
questions.explain: Anselm defines God as 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived', arguing such a being must exist in reality, not merely in the mind.

questions.q: Which statement best characterises the materialist view of the mind?
options: The mind is the form of the body but survives death
The mind is an immaterial substance separable from the body
The soul pre-exists the body and is immortal
Mental states are nothing over and above physical states of the brain and body
questions.explain: Materialism holds that the mind is not a separate substance but is identical to, or wholly dependent on, physical brain states.

questions.q: Which is a recognised challenge to the reliability of religious experience?
options: The cosmological argument
Naturalistic explanations from psychology (e.g. Freud) and neuroscience suggesting internal causes
Aquinas's analogy
The principle of credulity
questions.explain: Critics argue religious experiences may be products of psychological need or brain states rather than genuine encounters with God.

questions.q: How does the evidential problem of evil differ from the logical problem?
options: It claims a strict logical contradiction
It argues that the amount and distribution of suffering makes God's existence improbable rather than impossible
It concerns the definition of God
It denies that evil exists
questions.explain: The evidential problem treats evil, especially gratuitous suffering, as strong evidence against God rather than a strict contradiction.

questions.q: What objection did J.S. Mill raise against the design argument?
options: That the universe is eternal
That language about God is meaningless
That the cruelty and waste in nature count against a benevolent designer
That God is the greatest conceivable being
questions.explain: Mill argued that nature commits acts of horror and suffering that no good designer would be expected to produce.

questions.q: The via negativa (apophatic way) approaches language about God by:
options: Treating God-talk as expressing emotion
Verifying claims empirically
Saying only what God is not, since God transcends human description
Describing God through positive analogies
questions.explain: The via negativa preserves God's transcendence by denying limiting human attributes, asserting only what God is not.

questions.q: Which criticism of the cosmological argument did Russell express in his debate with Copleston?
options: That the design of the eye proves God
That evil is logically incompatible with God
That God is the greatest conceivable being
That the universe is 'just there, and that's all', requiring no further explanation
questions.explain: Russell rejected the demand for a cause of the universe as a whole, saying it is simply a 'brute fact'.
